pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Name three bugs from the exercise that compiled cleanly but were caught by go vet or staticcheck. For each: why couldn't the compiler catch it?
expected_points: printf verb mismatch: variadic ...any type-checks any argument against any verb
copied mutex via value receiver: copying a struct is legal semantics, but the copy's lock guards nothing
discarded context cancel: the language never requires a returned function to be called
malformed struct tag, deprecated API, or dead code as further examples — all legal strings/calls/declarations
vet and staticcheck check facts about meaning and usage, not language legality

questions.prompt: Walk me through the .golangci.yml you wrote: what does each part do, and how do you read a finding line from `golangci-lint run`?
expected_points: one binary running many linters in parallel with caching, configured at the repo root
default: none plus an explicit enable list means every linter is a deliberate choice, keeping findings signal
a finding reads file:line:col, message, then the producing linter in parentheses — the linter name is where to look up docs
errcheck caught unchecked error returns that neither vet nor staticcheck reported

questions.prompt: Your module requires sampler v1.3.1, a dependency requires v1.3.0, and v1.9.0 is the newest release. Which version builds, and why? And what does go.sum guarantee about it?
expected_points: v1.3.1 — minimal version selection takes the maximum of the required minimums
never v1.9.0: Go does not silently take the newest; upgrades happen only via explicit go get
deterministic and reproducible from go.mod alone, no dependency solver
go.sum stores content hashes: a later download with different bits fails the build — integrity and tamper evidence, not version selection

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a CPU profile and a heap profile, and what symptom would send you to each?
expected_points: CPU profile: sampled call stacks showing where execution time goes — reach for it when the program is slow
heap profile: sampled allocation sites showing where memory comes from — reach for it when memory grows or GC pressure dominates
obtained via go test -cpuprofile/-memprofile (or net/http/pprof on servers) and read with go tool pprof
profile before optimizing — guesses about hot spots are unreliable

questions.prompt: Pick the right command and justify it: (a) go.mod lists a dependency nothing imports anymore; (b) your app should build against a local checkout of your library; (c) you need the exact version of a dependency in use; (d) generated code is stale after its source changed.
expected_points: a: go mod tidy — syncs go.mod/go.sum with actual imports
b: go work — a workspace overrides module resolution locally without editing go.mod
c: go list -m <module> or go list -m all — asks the build itself
d: go generate ./... — reruns //go:generate directives

questions.prompt: In `go tool pprof -top`, what do the flat and cum columns mean, and what does it tell you when a function has large cum but tiny flat?
expected_points: flat: time spent in the function's own code; cum: including everything it called
large cum with tiny flat means the function delegates — the work happens in its callees
in the exercise, JoinNaive's time shows up as runtime allocation/copy work attributed up to it through cum

questions.prompt: A linter finding is a false alarm in context. What is the disciplined way to suppress it, and what does a bare `//nolint` cost the team?
expected_points: target the specific linter and state a reason: //nolint:errcheck // why
a bare //nolint suppresses every linter on that line indefinitely and explains nothing
each suppression is a reviewable decision; unexplained ones hide future real findings
